analysis.one_liner: Temporarily eliminates federal tax on capital gains for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors, never left the House Ways and Means Committee, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have wiped out the federal tax on capital gains — profit from selling stocks, businesses, real estate, and other investment assets — for two years. Anyone who sold an asset during that window would owe no federal income tax on the profit. It never received a hearing or a vote and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People and institutions with taxable investment gains. A two-year capital gains exclusion delivers its largest benefit to those with the largest sales: investors, wealthy households, fund managers, business owners, and other holders of capital assets. Middle-class households with modest capital gains would gain a smaller amount. The Treasury would forgo the revenue.

how_it_helps.text: The bill excludes gain from the sale or exchange of any capital asset from gross income, so sellers of stocks, businesses, real estate, and other investment property would owe no federal income tax on the profit for two years [S2] [S3].
The exclusion is temporary and terminates two years after enactment, applying to sales after the date of enactment [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, because the Treasury would collect less revenue during the exclusion window and other taxpayers or future borrowing would eventually cover the gap. The benefit flows overwhelmingly to those who sell large capital assets, so the cost would effectively subsidize gains realized by wealthier households and investment funds.

drawbacks.text: A temporary capital gains holiday rewards waiting: investors with assets due to be sold can delay sales into the two-year window, so much of the revenue loss would go to transactions that would have happened anyway, with the tax rate temporarily zero [S3].

Because benefit scales with the size of the gain, the largest dollar value would flow to households and funds making the largest asset sales, while the lost revenue must be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill provides no benefit tied to wages, work, or hiring — it simply makes investment profit tax-free for two years. The cost is forgone federal revenue, and the benefit is concentrated among the households and institutions with the largest asset sales. An honest assessment: this is a targeted two-year windfall for holders of capital, framed as a job-creation measure without any employment requirement in the text.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuck Fleischmann introduced the bill on July 31, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action is recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers generally kept the revenue that the two-year capital gains exclusion would have cost; investors lost the chance at a two-year tax holiday on asset sales.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who would have covered the cost

for.name: Rep. Chuck Fleischmann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; attracted no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party joined and no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so no voting pattern exists to judge.

industries.industry: Investors, asset managers, and holders of capital assets
industries.note: The bill would have made two years of capital gains tax-free, a benefit that scales with the size of the asset sale. Its failure leaves ordinary capital gains rates in place.
